stem: A sponsor requests a multi-agent orchestration layer to triage support tickets. Discovery finds the underlying decision is satisfied by one assistant with two tools, at roughly a third of the proposed infrastructure cost. What should the architect do next?

opts.t: Build the multi-agent orchestration layer as specified, since the sponsor defined the target architecture directly.
Tell the sponsor the simpler design meets the decision, and name what the multi-agent layer would have given up.
Proceed to defining the accuracy target and evaluation set, without addressing the architecture the sponsor named.
Tell the sponsor the multi-agent layer cannot be justified and decline to propose an alternative design.

whyRight: Discovery already shows the multi-agent layer is not required, so the architect must say so and name the simpler design's trade-off. The problem licenses the pattern, not the reverse; once discovery has run, silence about that finding withholds a decision the sponsor is entitled to make.

whyWrong.A: Building the named layer delivers a system, but never tells the sponsor that a simpler design meets the same decision at lower cost.
whyWrong.C: Bounding the requirement is the right move only when no architecture has been named; here one has, and that mismatch still needs addressing first.
whyWrong.D: Declining to propose an alternative drops the part of the answer the sponsor most needs: a workable design and what it costs to skip.

t1Clause: requests a multi-agent orchestration layer to triage support tickets

stem: A sponsor sets a 92% accuracy target for a claims-triage assistant handling a dozen claim types, and states the cost of a missed high-value claim. No evaluation set has been defined. What should the architect do next?

opts.t: Move to design, since the accuracy target and the cost of an error are both already stated.
Return to the sponsor to establish the accuracy target and the cost of an error before anything else.
Select the highest-capability model available to maximize accuracy against the stated target.
Specify a held-out evaluation set stratified to match the real distribution of claim types before proceeding.

whyRight: The target and the error cost are already stated, but nothing yet says the evaluation set matches the real mix of claim types. A held-out set stratified to that mix is the missing piece; without it, no design can be verified as meeting the target.

whyWrong.A: Moving to design applies only once the evaluation set is also settled; here it is not, so an unstratified or absent set would misreport performance on the real claim mix.
whyWrong.B: The target and the error cost are already given in the stem; returning to establish them again ignores facts already on the table and stalls on a step already complete.
whyWrong.C: A more capable model addresses capability, not measurement; it does nothing to fix the missing evaluation set, which is the actual gap blocking a verifiable result.

t1Clause: No evaluation set has been defined

stem: An assistant classifying support tickets scores within two points of 89% across every ticket category, evaluated on a stratified 2,000-case set. The account lead wants one accuracy figure for the board update. What should the architect provide?

opts.t: Report the 89% figure as a single number, and state the evaluation method and the set it was measured against.
Break the figure out by ticket category regardless, and report the end-to-end outcome including human review steps.
Decline to give a single figure, since performance depends on which ticket category is under discussion.
Report the 89% figure to the board, without stating how it was measured or on what set.

whyRight: Performance is uniform across categories, so a single figure is honest rather than misleading — segmenting a number that does not vary adds noise, not clarity. What the figure still needs is its measurement basis: the method used and the set it was scored against.

whyWrong.B: Breaking out a figure that does not vary by category adds detail the situation does not call for and buries the one number the board actually asked for in noise.
whyWrong.C: Declining to quantify abandons the board's decision entirely; performance here is uniform enough that a defensible single number is available and should be given.
whyWrong.D: The figure itself is the right figure, but without the method and the evaluation set attached, the board has a number it cannot verify or act on.

t1Clause: scores within two points of 89% across every ticket category

stem: To hit a cost-reduction target, a product lead proposes removing human review from loan-decision outputs in a segment where a regulator requires a named person to attest to each decision. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Explain which specific decisions in that segment carry accountability, and what automating each would risk.
Approve the removal, but add enhanced logging and periodic sampling to catch errors in that segment after the fact.
Refuse to remove review on the attestation requirement, and state in measurable terms what the reviewed segment is worth.
Commit to a maximum automated-error rate for the segment, and remove review once the model stays under that threshold.

whyRight: The regulator's attestation requirement is external and does not trade against a savings target; removing the named-person review breaks that constraint regardless of accuracy. The right response refuses on that basis and gives the segment's worth in measurable terms, not a promise to revisit later.

whyWrong.A: Naming the decisions and their risk explains the limit accurately, but leaves the actual proposal, removing review to hit a savings target, neither refused nor answered.
whyWrong.B: Sampling decisions after the fact catches errors once shipped; the attestation requirement calls for a person in the loop before the decision, not a log of it afterward.
whyWrong.D: An error-rate ceiling is an accuracy guarantee; the attestation requirement is about accountability, not accuracy, so meeting a threshold does not satisfy what the regulator actually requires.

t1Clause: a product lead proposes removing human review from loan-decision outputs

stem: A successful 40-user pilot of a document-review assistant is approved for rollout to 800 users, and human review absorbed 12% of pilot volume. Select two safeguards to apply before rollout.

opts.t: List which input, support-load, and edge-case assumptions may not hold at the new scale, and rebuild the cost model.
Convert the review proportion observed in the pilot into a staffing line sized to the projected rollout volume.
Size infrastructure capacity and rate limits for the new volume, and treat that as the binding constraint on rollout readiness.
Plan for a rare failure mode as routine at the new volume, whether or not it appeared during the pilot.

whyRight: Scaling to twenty times the pilot's users widens the input mix in ways the pilot never tested, so the assumptions behind it must be re-examined before the cost model is rebuilt. The review load actually measured in the pilot is the only sound basis for staffing at the new volume.

whyWrong.C: Sizing infrastructure capacity is real and necessary, but it is explicitly not the binding constraint; the input distribution behind the assumption audit is what actually bites at scale.
whyWrong.D: Planning for routine failure is the right move only once a rare failure has actually recurred in evidence; applying it with no observed trigger is a guess, not a safeguard.

t1Clause: human review absorbed 12% of pilot volume

stem: A document-classification contract restricts a client to a fixed, actively monitored set of document categories, with any change requiring a signed amendment. The client's legal team asks whether the accuracy commitment can be written more tightly than usual.

opts.t: Commit the same broadly segmented figure, with the scoring method, cadence, and exclusions stated as usual.
Decline to tighten the commitment, since the client's document mix cannot be reliably monitored.
Omit any accuracy commitment, since a fixed category set could still be amended later.
Offer a tighter accuracy commitment, since the client's input mix is now a controlled variable.

whyRight: The stem states the document mix is now fixed and actively monitored, which removes the one variable the provider normally cannot control. Once that variable is controlled, a tighter accuracy commitment is defensible, rather than the broad, segmented commitment built for an open, unpredictable population.

whyWrong.A: This is the right structure when the input mix is still open and uncontrolled; here the mix is stated as fixed and monitored, so a tighter figure is achievable instead.
whyWrong.B: The stem states the category set is actively monitored, directly contradicting the premise that the mix cannot be reliably monitored.
whyWrong.C: A fixed category set is still amendable in principle, but that risk does not justify dropping the commitment entirely when the variable driving it is now controlled.

t1Clause: a fixed, actively monitored set of document categories

stem: After a flawless early demo, a support assistant's only ongoing quality signal is about forty user complaints a month posted in a shared channel, none logged against a stored input, expected output, or reviewer, while leadership still expects demo-level performance.

opts.t: Establish a recurring review that reports real production performance against the agreed acceptance criteria.
Restructure the channel to capture input, output, expected output, and reviewer, feeding the evaluation set.
Assign an engineer to read every channel message each week and flag the most concerning cases.
Stop collecting complaints through the shared channel entirely, since anecdotal reports carry no usable frequency data.

whyRight: The presenting gap is that complaints are never logged as a stored input, output, expected output, and reviewer, so nothing can be measured or prioritized. Restructuring the channel into that structured capture, feeding each case into the evaluation set, is the fix a chat channel alone cannot provide.

whyWrong.A: A recurring review answers inflated expectations once real numbers exist to report; here there is no structured data yet, since nothing is logged as input, output, expected output, or reviewer.
whyWrong.C: Reading messages weekly surfaces individual cases but does not create the stored records needed to measure or prioritize failures by frequency.
whyWrong.D: The channel is the only quality signal available; removing it leaves no mechanism at all rather than repairing the one already in place.

t1Clause: none logged against a stored input, expected output, or reviewer

stem: Eight months after handover, the operations team maintaining a deployed claims-triage assistant proposes a prompt revision to cut response length, with a release scheduled for Friday and no rollback window before Monday's SLA reporting cycle.

opts.t: Provide fresh interface contracts, configuration rationale, failure modes, and gating tests as a full handover package.
Ship the revision on schedule and monitor production error rates closely for the first week afterward.
Require the regression tests named in the implementation guidance to pass before the revised prompt ships.
Have the operations lead manually compare a handful of sample outputs before and after the change.

whyRight: The scenario is a specific post-handover change with a fixed ship date. The implementation guidance exists precisely to gate this moment: the regression tests it names must pass before the change ships, catching a silent behavioral regression the deadline pressure would otherwise wave through.

whyWrong.A: This is the full handover bundle owed at first transfer, eight months too late; it does not gate the specific change already proposed and scheduled to ship.
whyWrong.B: Monitoring error rates afterward finds a regression only once it has already shipped, instead of the named tests catching it before release.
whyWrong.D: A handful of manually compared samples is not the systematic, named test suite the guidance requires to pass before any change ships.

t1Clause: proposes a prompt revision to cut response length, with a release scheduled for Friday and no rollback window before Monday's SLA reporting cycle

stem: Three months after launch, a compliance-review assistant's automated error rate holds steady at two percent while the volume of analyst complaints about answer quality has tripled, with the quarterly board update due in one week.

opts.t: Check for a shift in the input distribution and re-run the evaluation suite before the update.
Conclude the underlying model has degraded and roll back to the previous prompt version before the board update.
Recognize that the evaluation set has not been refreshed since launch and update it before drawing conclusions.
Add a temporary second reviewer to the queue and postpone re-running the evaluation suite until next quarter.

whyRight: The stem's own numbers show the mismatch: error rate flat at two percent while complaints have tripled, exactly the pattern where quality has degraded without showing up in operational telemetry. Checking for input-distribution shift and re-running the evaluation suite is the diagnostic step that tests for silent degradation directly.

whyWrong.B: The stem states the automated error rate is flat at two percent; rolling back on the premise that the model itself has degraded contradicts that stated number.
whyWrong.C: Refreshing a stale evaluation set is the right fix once one is confirmed stale; nothing in the stem establishes that yet, only the complaint-versus-telemetry gap.
whyWrong.D: Extra review capacity manages the symptom for one more quarter without running the diagnostic step that would explain why complaints are rising now.

t1Clause: the volume of analyst complaints about answer quality has tripled
